title: Two offers in one afternoon
note: Fictional patient and family. Values are illustrative, not targets. Philippine law, DOH orders and the PhilHealth circular are summarized as the module states them; the transplant center, its ethics committee and the attending nephrologist decide every step.
intro:
You are the nephrology fellow in the outpatient clinic of a tertiary hospital in Malolos, Bulacan. Mr. Ernesto Galang, 45, a jeepney driver with type 2 diabetes, has chronic kidney disease (CKD). His estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) has fallen from 23 to 16 mL/min per 1.73 m² in 13 months, and his albuminuria is heavy. He has no dialysis access. No doctor has ever mentioned transplantation to him.

His wife, Marites, 43, and his nephew, Jayson, 26, came with him. Jayson is an overseas Filipino worker (OFW) who flies back to Qatar in four weeks. Your references are the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) 2020 candidate and 2017 living donor guidelines, the Department of Health (DOH) rules on donation, and your attending nephrologist.

n1.prompt: Ernesto asks, “Dialysis na ba ako, Doc?” What is your plan for transplantation?

choices.text: Order the recipient tests available here first, and send the transplant referral once the results are back in about three months.
choices.feedback: The tests are useful, but the transplant center sets the checklist. Three months is a large share of the window he has left before dialysis. Refer now and let the work-up run alongside.
choices.then: You send the referral to the transplant center that afternoon, explain to Ernesto why now, and ask the access surgeon to see him as a safety net.

vitals.plan: Referred to transplant center; access planned

choices.text: Refer him to a transplant center this week, explain why it cannot wait, and still plan his dialysis access.
choices.feedback: His eGFR is falling about 7 a year with heavy albuminuria, so dialysis may come within the year. KDIGO 2020 advises referral at least 6 to 12 months before anticipated dialysis (Not Graded) and prefers pre-emptive living-donor transplantation. Access stays in the plan because a pre-emptive transplant may not happen in time.

vitals.plan: Referred to transplant center; access planned

choices.text: Explain gently that with diabetes he is not a transplant candidate, and start preparing him for hemodialysis.
choices.feedback: This closes a door the guideline keeps open. KDIGO 2020 recommends that candidates with type 1 or type 2 diabetes be considered for transplantation (1B), and age or diabetes alone does not exclude him.
choices.then: You send the referral to the transplant center that afternoon, explain to Ernesto why now, and ask the access surgeon to see him as a safety net.

vitals.plan: Referred to transplant center; access planned

choices.text: Plan hemodialysis first, and refer him once he has been stable on dialysis for three months.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2020 allows referral of stable dialysis patients, but waiting gives up the pre-emptive option. Longer time on dialysis before transplant is associated with worse graft and patient outcomes.
choices.then: You send the referral to the transplant center that afternoon, explain to Ernesto why now, and ask the access surgeon to see him as a safety net.

vitals.plan: Referred to transplant center; access planned

n2.scene: The transplant center sends its recipient checklist. Ernesto looks at the list and asks what all the tests are for.
n2.prompt: What evaluation plan do you write?

choices.text: An echocardiogram; if it is normal, tell him he is cleared for transplant and the team only needs to find a donor.
choices.feedback: One test does not answer the cardiac question in a diabetic candidate, and you do not declare anyone “cleared.” The transplant team weighs every risk together and decides.
choices.then: You rewrite the plan by domain: immunologic tests through the center, cardiac evaluation with non-invasive coronary screening, HIV and hepatitis B and C, latent tuberculosis, strongyloides, dental review and a question about herbal products.

vitals.plan: Recipient work-up under way, domain by domain

choices.text: Blood group, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) typing, HIV and hepatitis screening, and a cardiac work-up; leave everything else to the center.
choices.feedback: The core is right, but it misses the Philippine adjustments. Immunosuppression can reactivate latent tuberculosis and turn silent strongyloides into hyperinfection, and dental sepsis and herbal products are easy to miss.
choices.then: You rewrite the plan by domain: immunologic tests through the center, cardiac evaluation with non-invasive coronary screening, HIV and hepatitis B and C, latent tuberculosis, strongyloides, dental review and a question about herbal products.

vitals.plan: Recipient work-up under way, domain by domain

choices.text: Domain by domain: immunologic tests through the center, cardiac evaluation with non-invasive coronary screening, HIV and hepatitis B and C, latent tuberculosis, strongyloides, dental review, and herbal products.
choices.feedback: Each risk is something the graft or the operation must survive, so each is checked on its own. As a diabetic he is a high-risk candidate, and KDIGO 2020 suggests non-invasive coronary screening for asymptomatic high-risk candidates (2C). Tuberculosis and strongyloides matter more here than in the guideline’s source countries.

vitals.plan: Recipient work-up under way, domain by domain

n3.scene: Jayson comes back with his mother, Ernesto’s sister. He wants to donate “before my flight.” One clinic blood pressure is 140/88 mm Hg, and his body mass index is about 31 kg/m². His mother says, “Utang niya kay Ernesto ang pag-aaral niya.” Marites has said she wants to be tested too.
n3.prompt: How do you handle Jayson’s offer?

choices.text: Start a full donor evaluation with no deadline. Measure his pressure properly and check kidney function, albuminuria and glucose. A team member who does not care for Ernesto takes his consent alone, and he can withdraw at any time.
choices.feedback: The donor is a second patient. One reading is not hypertension, and KDIGO 2017 judges blood pressure, weight and age together against a lifetime risk. KDIGO 2017 asks for consent without the recipient present, and DOH Administrative Order (AO) 2021-0059 adds a psychiatric or psychological assessment and Hospital Transplant Ethics Committee approval. “Utang” is a warning sign of family pressure.

vitals.donor: Jayson: full evaluation, no deadline; Marites to be tested

choices.text: Arrange every donor test this week so the evaluation and the surgery can be finished before his flight to Qatar.
choices.feedback: A rushed donor evaluation is unsafe, and the flight sets no medical timetable. A family asking to fast-track a donor before a contract or flight is one of the module’s reasons to stop and call the attending.
choices.then: The attending nephrologist agrees with a plan you then write: Jayson’s evaluation starts without a deadline, a team member who does not care for Ernesto meets him alone, and he is told he can withdraw at any time.

vitals.donor: Jayson: full evaluation, no deadline; Marites to be tested

choices.text: Take his consent today with Ernesto and the family present, since in a Filipino family this is a shared decision.
choices.feedback: Pressure is invisible when the recipient and the family are in the room. KDIGO 2017 asks for consent in the absence of the intended recipient, and AO 2021-0059 requires consent witnessed by people unrelated to donor or recipient.
choices.then: The attending nephrologist agrees with a plan you then write: Jayson’s evaluation starts without a deadline, a team member who does not care for Ernesto meets him alone, and he is told he can withdraw at any time.

vitals.donor: Jayson: full evaluation, no deadline; Marites to be tested

choices.text: Tell him his blood pressure and weight rule him out, and move straight on to testing Marites.
choices.feedback: This may spare him, but it decides too early. KDIGO 2017 individualizes these findings after proper measurement; the evaluation, not one clinic visit, should answer the question.
choices.then: The attending nephrologist agrees with a plan you then write: Jayson’s evaluation starts without a deadline, a team member who does not care for Ernesto meets him alone, and he is told he can withdraw at any time.

vitals.donor: Jayson: full evaluation, no deadline; Marites to be tested

n4.scene: As the family leaves, the neighbor who drove them stops you in the corridor. “Doc, kung hindi pwede si Jayson, ako na lang. Basta bayaran lang nila ang utang ko sa lending.”

choices.text: Tell him kindly that this is not allowed, and leave it there so he is not embarrassed.
choices.feedback: The words are right, but the work is not finished. An offer tied to payment goes to the attending the same day and is documented in his words; the attending decides with the Hospital Ethics Committee on any further reporting.
choices.then: You find the man again, tell him calmly that the law does not allow a kidney in exchange for money or any help, do not take his name for any list, call the attending the same day and write down what he said.

choices.text: Suggest the family look into a transplant abroad, where arranging a paid donor may be easier.
choices.feedback: That is transplant tourism, which the Declaration of Istanbul condemns, and DOH policy is committed to that declaration. A patient asking about transplantation abroad is itself a reason to call the attending.
choices.then: You find the man again, tell him calmly that the law does not allow a kidney in exchange for money or any help, do not take his name for any list, call the attending the same day and write down what he said.

choices.text: Let him finish, tell him the law does not allow a kidney in exchange for money or any help, do not refer him, report it to the attending today and document his words.
choices.feedback: Paying off his loan is a gratuity, which AO 2010-0018 forbids for living non-related donors and AO 2021-0059 treats as commercial donation. Arranging donation for payment may meet the definition of trafficking under Republic Act (RA) 11862. He is probably a decent man in financial trouble, so you refuse with respect.

choices.text: Take his name for the donor list; the ethics committee can judge whether the help with his loan is reasonable.
choices.feedback: No committee can approve payment for a kidney. Do not add him to any donor list or start tests; report and document instead.
choices.then: You find the man again, tell him calmly that the law does not allow a kidney in exchange for money or any help, do not take his name for any list, call the attending the same day and write down what he said.

n5.scene: Marites asks, “Doc, sagot ba ng PhilHealth lahat ito?”

choices.text: Yes. The PhilHealth Z benefit covers the whole transplant, including his anti-rejection medicines for life.
choices.feedback: The package covers immunosuppressants only in the induction phase, until 1 week after discharge. A family that expects lifelong drugs to be covered may face a gap that threatens the graft.
choices.then: You walk Marites through the Z benefit as printed in the circular and book her with the transplant center’s PhilHealth liaison and social worker.

vitals.cost: Z benefit explained; liaison and social worker booked

choices.text: Explain the Z benefit as printed in Circular 2026-0019: evaluation, both operations and induction drugs to a week after discharge, at contracted facilities, with pre-authorization before surgery. Later drugs are not covered; dialysis coverage returns if the graft fails. Book the liaison and social worker.
choices.feedback: Quote the circular as printed and have the liaison confirm its effective date on the date of service. Living-donor pre-authorization must be filed before surgery. Knowing dialysis coverage returns after graft failure removes a fear that keeps some families from transplant.

vitals.cost: Z benefit explained; liaison and social worker booked

choices.text: Say that PhilHealth has a kidney transplant package and that the center’s PhilHealth office will explain the details.
choices.feedback: Honest, but thin. She needs to plan now for long-term drugs and the pre-authorization timing, and to hear that dialysis coverage returns if the graft fails.
choices.then: You walk Marites through the Z benefit as printed in the circular and book her with the transplant center’s PhilHealth liaison and social worker.

vitals.cost: Z benefit explained; liaison and social worker booked

choices.text: Advise them to ask the transplant team for the cheapest package code so the benefit stretches further.
choices.feedback: The package code follows the induction agent the transplant team chooses, not the other way around. The benefit must never decide candidacy or the choice of drug.
choices.then: You walk Marites through the Z benefit as printed in the circular and book her with the transplant center’s PhilHealth liaison and social worker.

vitals.cost: Z benefit explained; liaison and social worker booked

end.title: Six weeks later
end.text: Ernesto is halfway through his recipient work-up, and his fistula is planned as a safety net. Jayson flew back to Qatar with his evaluation paused, not rushed, and the team’s word that he can continue on his next leave or withdraw without blame. Marites’s evaluation has begun with a different team member. Your note on the corridor offer is with the attending and the Hospital Ethics Committee.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Refer early. KDIGO 2020: at least 6 to 12 months before anticipated dialysis (Not Graded); diabetes does not exclude (1B); keep dialysis access as a safety net.
  • Evaluate one risk at a time, including latent tuberculosis and strongyloides, and never call a candidate “cleared” yourself.
  • The donor is a second patient: no deadline, consent taken alone by someone who does not care for the recipient, freedom to withdraw, ethics committee approval.
  • Any offer tied to payment: name the rule, do not refer, report to the attending the same day, document.
  • Quote PhilHealth as printed, including what the package does not cover.

See Who to refer, Living donor, Ethics and law and Benefits.
